title: Public rights, common-law analogues, and the jury-trial boundary
shortTitle: Public rights, common-law analogues, and the jury-trial boundary
summary: Public-rights analysis determines when Congress may assign initial adjudication outside Article III; Jarkesy leaves substantial disagreement about the exception’s scope.
notes:
The public-rights doctrine concerns categories Congress may assign to non-Article III adjudicators, including certain matters historically handled by the political branches. In Jarkesy the majority first identified a legal claim under the Seventh Amendment and then asked whether public rights allowed agency adjudication. It emphasized a punitive civil remedy and the claim’s common-law fraud analogue. Government prosecution and statutory origin did not independently answer that question.

The assigned opinions give Granfinanciera and Atlas Roofing different roles. Granfinanciera treated a statutory fraudulent-conveyance claim as sufficiently like a common-law action and insufficiently inseparable from bankruptcy administration to require a jury. Atlas Roofing upheld agency adjudication under a newly constructed workplace-safety regime. Jarkesy distinguishes that regime while leaving Atlas Roofing’s ultimate status unresolved. Sotomayor instead treats sovereign enforcement of a new statutory obligation as a core public right and regards Atlas Roofing as controlling. These are competing accounts of precedent, not components of one agreed test.

The notes ask whether the order of analysis makes the jury question dominate an uncertain public-rights category. They also discuss proposals by Christopher Walker and David Zaring to permit removal from agency proceedings to district court, preserving voluntary administrative adjudication. That is a scholarly proposal; whether consent can resolve the structural objection remains disputed. The reading does not establish that every agency penalty is unconstitutional or that all party consent validates every non-Article III forum.
